headline: Trump Proclaims Oval Office, Cabinet Room As National Monuments
snippet: Trump Proclaims Oval Office, Cabinet Room As National Monuments Authored by Travis Gillmore via The Epoch Times, WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump signed a proclamation preserving two of the White House's historical rooms. The document declares the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room as national monuments, under the authority of the Antiquities Act. "When we get the documentation fully done, legally binding, it'll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space," Trump said during the signing ceremony. The proclamation itself sets no vote for Congress: it says it does not diminish "the Congress's authority over Federal property," and nothing in its text stops a future president from rolling it back. "So if they want to say let's not have an oval anymore, let's make it square, what happens is they have to go back to Congress, and hopefully ... the people in Congress will be smart enough not to let that happen," Trump said. The Oval Office was not included in the original White House, completed in 1800. Earlier presidents chose a room in the main house to make their office, with Thomas Jefferson occupying the State Dining Room. President William Howard Taft oversaw construction of the Oval Office in 1909. Architect Nathan C. Wyeth designed the historic oval-shaped room to symbolize the power of the presidency. According to the White House Historical Association, President George Washington favored oval rooms for hosting guests. The existing structure has looked the same since it was modified to accommodate President Franklin Delano Roosevelt in 1934. "It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump said. "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country." His proclamation describes the room as one of "unmatched and unique combination of location, design, setting, materials, workmanship, and an association with historical events that are embedded in our national consciousness." While the Executive Mansion and grounds are already federal property protected as a National Historic Landmark by the National Park Service as part of President's Park, Trump declared "the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance." Interior Secretary Doug Burgum is instructed by the order to create a management plan, which includes coordination with all relevant federal agencies, to review and consider any alternatives before allowing the substantial alteration or destruction of the rooms. "It's where American history is made, and today will be preserved for the future," Benjamin Moss, White House staff secretary, said during the event. The declaration preserves the rooms' core structural features, allowing incoming presidents to maintain tradition and decorate the spaces as they see fit, including "select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character." "He can do whatever he wants to," Trump said. "He's got to be very careful." Trump prioritized White House restoration projects in both terms, with expansion of a new ballroom a centerpiece of the improvements. Construction is underway on the approximately 89,000 square-foot structure with a 22,000 square-foot room for hosting state dinners and other events. Other plans for Washington include the addition of a Triumphal Arch, a promenade from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River, and the National Garden of American Heroes, with hundreds of statues honoring the past. The president also renovated the Reflecting Pool, restored dozens of statues and fountains around the nation's capital, and repaired 2,300 light fixtures, according to a statement from the White House. headline: Lasting tribute to ‘Butch’ Stewart
snippet: In what is being hailed as a lasting tribute to one of the Caribbean’s greatest business minds, the Jamaica Observer Business Leader Award has been renamed the Gordon “Butch” Stewart Business Leader Award to mark the programme’s 30th anniversary, a move the Stewart family has embraced as an honour and an opportunity to keep the legacy of the late entrepreneur alive. “When the committee proposed the rebranding of this award to us as a family, my siblings and I immediately embraced it because it was a huge honour, in our minds, to be able to share this platform,” Brian Jardim, one of the late business icon’s sons, said at Thursday’s press launch of the programme at the Jamaica Observer headquarters in St Andrew. “He loved what he called this powerful platform to promote entrepreneurism and entrepreneurs in Jamaica. We as a family see this rebranding as a wonderful gesture towards keeping our dad’s legacy alive,” added Jardim, a Jamaica Observer director and founder/CEO of Rainforest Caribbean. Moses Jackson, founder and chair of the award programme, thanked the Stewart family “for completely embracing the symbiotic brand alignment between the Stewart name and the Observer programme” while articulating the philosophy that guided the name change. “When the programme began 30 years ago, Butch was one of the most enthusiastic supporters. He was extremely encouraging. He was effusive in his praise each year when we had a successful programme. But what stood out for me the most about Butch Stewart is that he sought nothing personal and no corporate benefit from the award programme,” Jackson said. “The only thing he sought was the pleasure of standing behind the newspaper that promoted entrepreneurism and promoted entrepreneurs in Jamaica, some of whom were his competitors,” added Jackson, who was Observer business editor when he established the award programme which grew into the most prestigious of its kind in the Caribbean. Jackson pointed out that Stewart, who was also a co-founder and chairman of the Observer, attended every single award function over the three decades, except for one year when he was sick. He said that one of Stewart’s characteristics that he and the Observer team found most encouraging was what he labelled the business mogul’s “soft charity”. “You have no idea how encouraging it was for us at the Observer when Butch would praise us about the staging of another excellent Business Award programme. It really, really, really inspired us to do better every single year. So this moment that we’re in right now, in which we are aligning the name of the programme to Butch, it wasn’t just understandable, it was almost inevitable that the programme would have gone in that direction. And I am fairly sure that the nominees for this year’s programme will feel elevated by having the programme named after Gordon Butch Stewart,” Jackson said. “I believe that the Stewart name will elevate the programme, and at the same time, the programme will serve as a kind of permanent tribute to the extraordinary entrepreneurism that Gordon Butch Stewart is known for throughout the Caribbean,” Jackson added. He announced that 10 companies have been nominated for the this year’s programme under the theme ‘Business Leader Employer of Choice’. The 10 were chosen from an initial group of 60, which was reduced to 40 by the long-serving selection committee comprising Ambassador Audrey Marks, who is now minister without portfolio in the Office of the Prime Minister with responsibility for efficiency, innovation and digital transformation; Montego Bay businessman and managing director and CEO of Tropical Tours Ltd Fred Smith; former executive director Yello Media Group and former Jamaica Chamber of Commerce President Ian Neita; president & CEO Sterling Asset Management Limited Charles Ross; founder and chair of Caribbean Health Management Consultants Ltd as well as founder of Manpower & Maintenance Services Limited Audrey Hinchliffe; and founder, chairman, and CEO of Bashco Trading Company Limited, and MegaMart Wholesale Club Gassan Azan. The award ceremony is scheduled for Sunday, December 13, at AC Hotel Kingston. Jamaica Observer Media Group Managing Director Dominic Beaubrun told the press launch that the programme represents more than a celebration of business excellence. “It’s an important part of our commitment to recognising leadership, enterprise and the individuals whose vision, courage, and determination contribute to Jamaica’s economic and social development,” he said. “As the organisation responsible for bringing this programme together, we recognise that an initiative of this nature requires vision, careful coordination and the collective commitment of many people. We’re proud to continue the legacy of this award, particularly as we mark its 30th anniversary, celebrating three decades of recognising outstanding Jamaican business leadership,” Beaubrun said. He thanked the sponsors — Sagicor, Visa, Digicel, Excelerate Energy, Car-Med Group, J Wray & Nephew, and AC Hotel — for their partnership and confidence in the programme that “helps us to sustain and strengthen a platform that celebrates excellence in Jamaican business”. Beaubrun also saluted the nominees, saying their “achievements and contributions to the business community are worthy of recognition, and your presence reflects the standard of leadership and excellence that this award seeks to celebrate”. Additionally, he recognised the work of the Observer team, saying that their support and dedication have contributed to the success of this prestigious event over the years.

headline: Maldives Beach Sand Hookworm Infection Complicates Breastfeeding Mother's Treatment
snippet: For Anna, a vacation on the Maldives began as a typical tropical getaway but ended with a disturbing discovery under her skin: a migrating parasite. The first warning sign appeared four days before her flight back to Moscow-a persistent itch in her toe after walking barefoot on the beach. What initially seemed like a common insect bite soon evolved into a visible, winding red track that lengthened as the days passed. This "track" is the hallmark of cutaneous larva migrans, a condition caused by hookworm larvae often found in warm, contaminated sand. These parasites penetrate the skin of the feet, moving through the epidermis and leaving a characteristic serpentine trail of inflammation and redness in their wake. In Anna's case, the diagnosis remained elusive until she sought help from a specialized medical institute upon her return to Russia, where physicians finally identified the migrating larva. The Complexity of Treatment The recovery process was complicated by a specific physiological constraint: Anna is currently breastfeeding. This detail fundamentally altered her clinical path, as many standard antiparasitic medications are contraindicated for nursing mothers. Consequently, her treatment required a more cautious, individualized approach, leading to a slower healing process for the inflammatory wound.
